Count the 404 errors in a log

cat access.log | grep 404 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Workstation & editor · 2/5

The pipe connects two commands

cat access.log | grep 404

  • cat access.log writes the file to its standard output
  • | connects that output to the next command's standard input
  • grep 404 reads the lines from its standard input

Workstation & editor · 3/5

Each stage changes the text

cat7 lines
grep 4045 lines
sort5 lines, grouped
uniq -c2 counted lines
sort -rnlargest first

Workstation & editor · 4/5

The answer: which pages fail most

404 /old3 errors
404 /logo.png2 errors

Workstation & editor · 5/5

Redirection order decides where errors go

ls > out.txt 2>&1

  • stdout goes to out.txt
  • stderr copies stdout: out.txt

ls 2>&1 > out.txt

  • stderr copies stdout: the terminal
  • then stdout moves to out.txt

Redirections run left to right.

We count the 404 errors in a small web server log.

Seven lines go in at the left.

The pipe symbol connects the output of one

command to the input of the next.

Here, grep reads what cat writes.

Watch the number of lines change at each stage of the pipeline.

Cat sends seven lines, grep keeps five, sort groups them, uniq counts

two groups, and the last sort puts the largest count first.

The final output shows the count for each page.

Slash old fails three times, and slash logo dot png fails twice.

Bash processes redirections from left to right, so their order matters.

On the left, ls sends both streams to out.txt.

On the right, the error stays on the terminal.
